summary:
Bogotá Capital District stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the more developed legal regimes for trans people in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official who defended the change described those examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and a 2012 Constitutional Court ruling allowed the change to be recorded at the civil registry without a family court.

Marriage equality has been available since April 2016, when Colombia became the fourth Latin American country to legalise same-sex marriage, and adoption by same-sex couples since November 2015. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, and a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. Rulings T-033 of 2022 and T-527 of 2024 protected the right to gender identity and its recording. National identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers, with the documentation framework recognising four identity markers: female, male, trans and non-binary. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Detention carries specific protections. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system, and a 2012 ruling allowed a transgender woman to choose her own hairstyle and makeup in prison.

Within the district, the operative screening reality is mass identity-check operation. More than 200 officers were deployed in San Bernardo in April 2025, and over 1,200 uniformed officers carrying out background and migrant control operated in Santa Fe in January 2026. A visibly gender-nonconforming person in central Bogotá is therefore statistically likely to be stopped and asked for identification, which places the accuracy and presentation of one's documents at the centre of daily risk.

Bogotá has the best-documented trans community and services in the country, alongside a documented police-violence pattern in its tolerance zone. Red Comunitaria Trans, a trans community organisation, reported police shouting at, baton-beating and shooting at trans sex workers in the early hours on a central street; the district mayor's office took up the case.

Lethal violence reaches the capital. Two trans women were killed within hours of each other on the night of 2 January 2026, and a 32-year-old trans activist was found dead in the hills at the urban fringe in December 2023.
tangentialFactors:
The district sits inside a national pattern of lethal violence against trans and gender-nonconforming people. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one count put 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten and thrown into a creek in Bello, Antioquia, on 4 April 2025; a video of the assault circulated from 5 April, and her mother Sandra Borja stated that they killed her for being who she was. President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and vigils were held in several cities. CNN covered attacks against LGBTQ people in the country in August 2025 in the context of the same case.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that rising killings must be addressed urgently. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity.

The sharpest risk outside the capital sits where armed groups operate. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyers targeting drug addicts, prostitutes and gay men, and threatened a further wave; trans women there reported few options beyond sex work, one trans salon owner was forced to relocate twice after death threats, and a friend of another trans woman was killed. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under wording that named trans people among military targets.

Despite the anti-discrimination laws, prejudice and discrimination against LGBTI people remain present in a considerable part of the population. That gap is what a gender-nonconforming visitor meets in practice: a strong statutory framework, contested daily on the street and at checkpoints.
localsOnly:
Residents change their legal gender marker by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015, with the recording handled at the civil registry under the 2012 Constitutional Court ruling. The documentation framework offers four markers — female, male, trans and non-binary — on the national identity card, and rulings T-033 of 2022 and T-527 of 2024 protect the recording of gender identity.

Community infrastructure is the district's defining feature for residents. Red Comunitaria Trans documents police conduct against trans sex workers and has carried complaints to the district mayor's office, which took up the case. Pride parades in Bogotá rank among the country's large LGBTQ events, and the district has thriving gay neighbourhoods. Claudia López Hernández became the first openly gay person to serve as mayor of Bogotá.

Residents deprived of liberty hold specific rights: a 2012 ruling permitted a transgender woman to choose her own hairstyle and makeup in prison, and a subsequent court ruling addressed the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty more broadly.

A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, so protections currently rest on Constitutional Court jurisprudence, the 2011 anti-discrimination law and administrative rules rather than a single consolidated statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The date on which trans and non-binary markers became available on national identification documents is unresolved across the sources: one gives November 2025, another states the options are offered beginning in 2026. A visitor relying on a specific marker on entry should verify the current position with Colombian consular or migration authorities.

No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or migration screening of trans travellers, including how gender markers mismatched between a passport and a Colombian record are handled at Bogotá's airport. The identity-check figures cited here concern ground operations in San Bernardo and Santa Fe, not border control.

The national homicide figures come from different sources covering different periods — 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 and 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 — and are not directly comparable or additive. Several overview claims rest on encyclopaedic sources rather than primary legal texts.

The status of the comprehensive trans law is stated only as of 2025; whether it has advanced or been enacted since is not sourced here.

Medical care access, hormone supply and airport security treatment for trans passengers are not covered by any source in this inventory.
